name: Nyamwezi
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Nyamwezi (nyam1276) is not in the catalog. The sweep listed one title, Dahl 1904 'Die Töne und Akzente im KiNamwezi' (MSOS 7, Abt. III: 106-126, Glottolog 132479); the whole MSOS vol. 7 was already on file from archive.org (item mitteilungen07berluoft) and I re-read the accent section and verified it on the p.121 page image. Dahl separates pitch tone (pp. 106-120) from dynamic accent (pp. 121-126) and states that main and secondary accent can fall on any syllable, that the most frequent pattern is penultimate main accent + final secondary accent (prefix takes the main accent with monosyllabic stems), and lists further combinations with main accent as far left as the sixth-from-last syllable. This is the best first-hand stress statement for the language read in this sweep; there is no catalog coding to confirm or contradict. Nothing remained unread among the sweep items (priority none). the on-disk already lists unopened later works (Nurse & Maganga 1979; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 body; Schadeberg 1989/2005; Steere 1882) whose stress content is unknown. Saved this sweep: Glottolog record and archive.org metadata JSON plus a dated addendum in

new_statements.quote: Der Haupt-, ebenso wie der Nebenakzent kann auf jeder Silbe gefunden werden: [...] Wie zu jedem Berg ein Tal gehört, so ist das Auftreten des Haupttones ohne Nebenton undenkbar. Absolut einsilbige Wörter sind deshalb jedes Akzentes bar. Die häufigste Form des Auftretens ist die, daß bei zweisilbigen Wörtern (bzw. dreisilbigen, aber zweisilbigen Stämmen) Penultima den Hauptakzent, Ultima den Nebenakzent bekommt [...]. Dementsprechend erhält bei nur einsilbigen Stämmen das Verbal- oder Nominalpräfix den Hauptakzent, der eigentliche Stamm dagegen nur den Nebenakzent, vorausgesetzt, daß er ohne angehängtes Suffix, Enklitik usw. tatsächlich die Ultima bildet.
new_statements.translation: The main accent, like the secondary accent, can be found on any syllable: [...] As every mountain has its valley, so the occurrence of the main accent without a secondary accent is unthinkable. Strictly monosyllabic words therefore have no accent at all. The most frequent pattern is that in disyllabic words (or trisyllabic words with disyllabic stems) the penult receives the main accent and the ultima the secondary accent [...]. Accordingly, with monosyllabic stems the verbal or nominal prefix receives the main accent and the stem itself only the secondary accent, provided that, without an added suffix, enclitic etc., it actually forms the ultima.
new_statements.citation: Dahl, E[dmund]. 1904. Die Töne und Akzente im Kinamwezi. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin 7, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 106-126.
new_statements.locator: p. 121, section 'Die Akzente im Kinamwezi' (archive.org item mitteilungen07berluoft, leaf n694)

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked the held page image (running head 'Dahl: Die Töne und Akzente im Kiṅamwezi. 121') and the scanned slice lines 1259-1301. The section heading 'Die Akzente im Kiṅamwezi' and every quoted sentence are on p.121 as quoted; the only differences are (a) the report's '[...]' elides the schema list 1a-e/2a-e and the phrase 'bekommt, also ˘́˘̀ bzw. ˘˘́˘̀', and (b) the print reads 'bei nur einsilbigen Stimmen' (a printer's error) where the quote silently normalizes to 'Stämmen'. Reading: I agree with tonal-with-stress-statement. Dahl's article is in two parts: pp.106-120 'Die eigentlichen Töne im Kinamwezi' state where the Hochton and Tiefton fall (contracted genitive regens ultima, monosyllab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dahl (a Moravian missionary at Urambo) separates pitch tones ('eigentliche Töne', with a Hochton whose positions he lists) from dynamic accents. He says main and secondary accent can occur on any syllable, but the default is main accent on the penultimate and secondary on the final syllable (so the prefix carries the main accent when the stem is monosyllabic); pp.122-126 then list six other main/secondary combinations, including accent on the 4th-, 5th- and 6th-last syllables in long derived verbs and reduplications. His accented examples (e.g. ku-fwilá, vafwá, ku-göngola) look like the H-tone / high-tone-shift patterns that Schadeberg (1991) and Kanijo (2019) describe, so the 'accent' is probably not independent of tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: every polysyllabic word has both a Hauptakzent and a Nebenakzent; default Nebenakzent on the ultima when the main accent is penultimate; other placements listed in groups I-VI.
new_statements.exceptions: Any syllable may bear either accent; groups II-VI list antepenultimate and earlier main accents (long extended verbs, full reduplications, e.g. ku-gelekelezya, ku-yanukulizya). Meinhof 1904 (same volume, p.241), working from four speakers, contradicts Dahl: the lengthening ('mechanical') accent 'seems to prefer the antepenult and to stay on the initial syllable even in four-syllable words', but 'the rule is not clear to me'. Modern descriptions (Schadeberg 1991; Kanijo 2019; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 per its TOC) describe Nyamwezi purely as a two-tone language with high tone shift and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms and short phrases, Urambo/Kigalaganza dialect area (with Sisumbwa comparisons); Meinhof's remarks are from elicited isolated words. Confidence low: 1904 missionary description whose 'accent' marks likely conflate H tone; no modern source states a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Dahl 1904 describes the Nyamwezi of Urambo (Kigalaganza dialect, with Sisumbwa comparisons); Meinhof 1904 elicited from four Nyamwezi speakers in Germany/East Africa; Velten 1901 is the Unyanyembe dialect; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 and Kanijo 2019 describe the Ndala (Nzega District) variety. All are Nyamwezi proper (nyam1276); no separate glottocode assigned here for the Galaganza dialect.

new_statements.quote: Absolut einsilbige Wörter sind deshalb jedes Akzentes bar. Die häufigste Form des Auftretens ist die, daß bei zweisilbigen Wörtern (bzw. dreisilbigen, aber zweisilbigen Stämmen) Penultima den Hauptakzent, Ultima den Nebenakzent bekommt, also ˊˋ bzw. _ˊˋ. Dementsprechend erhält bei nur einsilbigen Stämmen das Verbal- oder Nominalpräfix den Hauptakzent, der eigentliche Stamm dagegen nur den Nebenakzent, vorausgesetzt, daß er ohne angehängtes Suffix, Enklitik usw. tatsächlich die Ultima bildet.
new_statements.translation: Absolutely monosyllabic words are therefore devoid of any accent. The most frequent pattern is that in disyllabic words (or trisyllabic words with disyllabic stems) the penult receives the main accent and the ultima the secondary accent, i.e. ˊˋ or _ˊˋ. Correspondingly, with monosyllabic stems the verbal or nominal prefix receives the main accent and the stem itself only the secondary accent, provided that, without an attached suffix, enclitic etc., it really forms the ultima.
new_statements.citation: Dahl, Edmund. 1904. Die Töne und Akzente im KiNamwezi. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin 7, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 106-126.
new_statements.reading: First-hand missionary description (Urambo dialect area, 1904): a dynamic main accent distinct from pitch tone; the commonest placement is penultimate main accent + final secondary accent, but Dahl states at the outset that both accents 'can be found on any syllable' and documents (pp. 122-126) main accent on the antepenult and further left, up to the sixth-from-last syllable, especially in reduplicated and long derived verb stems. So: penultimate-default with lexically variable placement, not a fixed penultimate rule. Meinhof 1904 (same volume, p. 241, also on file) independently reports a 'mechanische Ton' that in Namwezi 'seems to like to stand on the third-from-last syllable' but admits the rule was unclear to him; later tone-based work (Schadeberg 1991; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 TOC; Kanijo 2019) makes no stress statement.

sources.note: Two-part study: pp.106-120 'Die eigentlichen Töne' (positions of the Hochton = pitch), pp.121-126 'Die Akzente' (dynamic accent): main and secondary accent can fall on any syllable (ultima to 5th/6th-last); the commonest pattern is main accent on the penult and secondary on the ultima in disyllabic stems; with monosyllabic stems the prefix takes the main accent. Verified on page image.

sources.note: sec. 1.5.1 Basic phonology (pp.7-12): seven vowels with contrastive length, coalescence and glide formation; 1.5.1.3: 'Nyamwezi has two basic surface tones: low (unmarked) and high (marked with an acute accent). sources.note: Historical-comparative (spirantization, 7>5 vowels, Dahl's Law, lexicostatistics); the only prosodic remark is that 'it might be a rule in SSN which states that penultimate syllables tend to lengthen their vowels' (vowel-length discussion on Sukuma data). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 1991. High Tone Shift in KiNyamwezi. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 17S (Special Session on African Language Structures): 210-221.
sources.note: Tone paper (data with Clement Maganga): a high tone is realized one mora to the right of its underlying position; a single word-final H yields a final rising tone with concomitant vowel length; long vowels arise from coalescence and automatically before prenasalized consonants. No mention of stress, accent or penultimate prominence.
